en: The Sūtra on the Seven Stations and Three Contemplations Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
(I) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.
The Buddha said,
“Bhikṣus! The bhikṣus replied.
"So be it," the Buddha said. "Bhikṣus!"

Knowing seven bases and contemplating three bases, one swiftly attains liberation from the fetters through the Dharma of the Path; being free from fetters, the mind is liberated, having attained the Dharma through wisdom. Having seen the Dharma and realized it for oneself, birth is exhausted; having practiced the path with intention, having done what was to be done, one shall no longer return.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"What is meant by 'knowing the seven points'?
It is that a learned bhikṣu knows form as it truly is, knows the origin of form, knows the cessation of form, and knows the practice leading to the extinction of form."
One knows the gratification of form, one knows the suffering of form, and one knows the escape from form; one knows these with utmost sincerity.

Likewise, regarding feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness, one knows them as they truly are according to their original nature. One knows the origin of consciousness, one knows the cessation of consciousness, and one knows the path leading to the cessation of consciousness as it was originally known.

Furthermore, one knows the gratification of consciousness, one knows the suffering of consciousness, one knows the escape from consciousness, and one knows the original, sincere nature of consciousness.
What is the suchness of form as it truly is?
Form consists of the four great elements, and it also exists within the domain of the four great elements; form is fundamentally thus, and one knows it as it fundamentally is.
What is the knowledge of the origination of form as it was originally?
Craving is the origination of form; such is the knowledge of the origination of form. What is this knowledge?
The exhaustion of form is known as it truly is: the exhaustion of craving is the exhaustion of form; such is the exhaustion of form known as it truly is.
What is the exhaustion of the formations of form known as it truly is?

If form constitutes these eight factors— namely, the Noble Truths, Right View, and Right Concentration as the eighth— and if one thus practices the full understanding of form with sincerity and knowledge of its origin,
what is meant by "knowing the gratification of form with sincerity and knowledge"?
That form gives rise to delight and gives rise to desire—thus one knows the gratification of form as it truly is.
What is the distress of form, knowing it as it truly is?
That form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—thus one knows the distress of form as it truly is.
What is the essential knowledge of form as it truly is?
It is the ability to understand the desire and greed for form, to abandon that desire, and to transcend that desire; this is the essential knowledge of form as it truly is.
"What is meant by 'feeling' (vedanā)?
One is able to know six types of feeling:
the feeling arising from the eye-faculty, and the feelings arising from the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-faculties. This is what is meant by knowing feeling."
What is the origin of feeling?
The planting of conditions is the origin of feeling; such is the origin of feeling.
What is the full knowledge of the cessation of feeling?
When the planting [of sensations] is exhausted, the exhaustion of sensation and itching is fully known; such is the full knowledge of the exhaustion of sensation and itching.
What is the practice for the full experience of the exhaustion of sensation and itching?
If one practices the eightfold path—namely, right view through to right concentration as the eight—such is the path for the full experience of the exhaustion of sensation and itching.
What is the consciousness of the gratification of feeling?
It is the seeking, the pursuit, the longing for what is felt; such is the consciousness of the gratification of feeling, known as such.
What is the consciousness of the distress of feeling?
That which is felt as painful or pleasant is impermanent, subject to decay, and distressing to the mind; such is the knowledge of feelings as being distressing.
What is the essential nature of feelings?

That which craves for feelings to continue living is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); that which can sever craving and greed is self-deliverance (*ātma-paritrāṇa*). Such is the knowledge of the essential nature of feelings, to be known according to reality.
"What is mental volition? There are six types of mental volition pertaining to the body:
mental volition regarding the eye-base, and mental volition regarding the bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; such are the six types of mental volition pertaining to consciousness."
What is the habitual tendency toward volition?
The habitual tendency of planting is the habitual tendency toward volition; such is the habitual tendency toward volition.
What is the longing for volition?

Because evil leads to the experience of suffering, I therefore teach the relinquishing of bodily misconduct; if a bhikṣu has already relinquished bodily misconduct, he will obtain benefit and obtain peace.
"Therefore, I have taught the abandoning of bodily misconduct, and that of speech and mind is as explained above. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, having arrived at the Buddha's presence, he prostrated before the Buddha and sat down. Once seated, he asked the Buddha:
"What is it that is not guarded when the body is not guarded?
What is it that is not guarded when speech is not guarded?"
"What is meant by 'not guarding' and 'not guarding the mind'?
The Buddha then said:

"In the home of Anāthapiṇḍika, the mind does not guard bodily conduct, nor does it attain guarding of vocal conduct, nor does it attain guarding of mental conduct; it does not guard its own conduct, it does not guard the conduct of body and self, it does not guard the conduct of voice and self, and because it does not guard the conduct of mind and body, the body rots, speech rots, and mental conduct also rots."
If one’s bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and mental conduct have already become rotten, they are unwholesome; death will be unwholesome, and the state of rebirth will also be unwholesome.
Take, for example, Kātyāyana!

If a multi-storied house or a hall is not roofed, and rain falls upon it, the rafters will become soaked, the beams will become soaked, and the walls will become soaked. Once the walls are soaked, they rot; the beams rot, and the rafters rot as well. It is just like this.

Gṛhapati! If one does not guard one's own mind, nor guards one's bodily conduct, nor guards one's verbal conduct, nor guards one's mental formations, then because one does not guard the mind, voice, and body, it is unwholesome; at death it is unwholesome, and the state one receives after death is unwholesome.
The householder then asked the Buddha,
"What is the restraint by which one attains bodily restraint?
What is the restraint by which one attains verbal restraint?"
“What is meant by guarding so as to attain mindfulness and guard?
The Buddha told the householder:

“When the mind is already guarded, one seeks to guard the mindfulness of body and speech. By guarding one’s own body, guarding one’s own speech, and guarding one’s own mindfulness, then the body does not decay, the voice does not decay, and the mindfulness does not decay. Having practiced with an undecayed body, having practiced with an undecayed voice, and having practiced with an undecayed mindfulness, at the time of death one attains a good death, a good rebirth, and a good destination.”
An analogy, householder!

Suppose there is a multi-storied building or a hall with a roof covering; when rain falls, the rafters do not get soaked, the beams do not get soaked, and the walls do not get soaked. Since they are not soaked, the walls do not rot, the beams do not rot, and the rafters do not rot. Such is the analogy.

If one guards the mind, and likewise guards the body and guards speech—if one thus guards the mind, body, and speech—then at the time of death one dies well, one passes away well, and one attains a good destination.
The Buddha concluded from behind:
"For one who does not guard the mind, because of wrong doubt and because of sleepiness, Māra gains mastery.

Thus, you should simply guard the mind; if you wish to practice the Truths, you should simply practice the Truths. Furthermore, once you know what has emerged within, do not fall into sleepiness, and you will attain the severance of the root of suffering."
Thus spoke the Buddha. (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are three kinds of persons. What are the three?
The first class does not see with their eyes; the second class sees with one eye; the third class sees with two eyes.
What is it like to have no eyes at all?
Monks, it is like this world.

There are those who lack this faculty of vision: they think, "I shall acquire means of livelihood where none yet exist," or "I shall manage my livelihood," yet once it has been acquired, they squander it recklessly; nor do they possess this vision, thinking, "I shall practice giving" or "I shall cultivate merit, so that by these causes and conditions I may enjoy happiness in future lives and ascend to heaven. To have no such calculation is what is called being without vision.
"What is meant by 'one who has but one eye'?

Monks, in this world, one who has but one eye is one who possesses such an eye as this: 'May I obtain wealth that I have not yet obtained; may the wealth already obtained not diminish. Yet, despite having such an eye, he lacks another: 'I shall practice giving with a view toward illusion, and by reason of these causes and conditions, may I attain rebirth in heaven. Because he lacks such an eye, he is called 'one who has but one eye.'"
"What are these two eyes called? Monks, there is a person in the world who possesses this eye:

'May I acquire wealth that I have not yet acquired; having acquired it, may it not diminish. He possesses such an eye. Furthermore, he possesses this eye: 'May I practice generosity, and by reason of this cause and condition, may I ascend to heaven. He also possesses this eye. Such a person is called one who possesses the two eyes."

"Explaining from the end, it is said that the exhaustion of perception is the exhaustion of consciousness; when the root is exhausted, there is the exhaustion of perception and consciousness—this is what is meant by the exhaustion of perception and consciousness.
What is the practice for the realization of the exhaustion of perception and consciousness?"

These are the eight modes of consciousness through which consciousness cognizes. With the vision of truth as the eighth, one attains the concentration of mind upon truth; in this way, ideation, sensation, formations, and consciousness are all exhausted.
What is the consciousness of the relish of ideation?

That which is the perception of the gratification in volitional formations (*saṃskāra*)—namely, that they give rise to pleasure, satisfaction, and joy—is the perception of the gratification in volitional formations.
What is the perception of the affliction in volitional formations?
That which is the perception of volitional formations as impermanent, subject to exhaustion, suffering, and subject to change is the perception of the affliction in volitional formations.
What is the essential knowledge regarding volitional formations?

It is the understanding that the desire and greed for what one forms through volition can be resolved, the desire and greed can be severed, and the desire and greed can be transcended; such is the essential knowledge regarding volitional formations.
"What is the consciousness of birth and death?

It is the consciousness of birth and death within the six bases: the consciousness of birth and death in the eye-base, and likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases; such is the consciousness of birth and death."
What is the knowledge of the origin of birth and death?
The knowledge of the origin of birth and death is the knowledge of the origin [of consciousness].
What is the knowledge of the cessation of birth and death?
The exhaustion of planting is the consciousness of the exhaustion of birth and death.
What is the consciousness of practice for the desire for the exhaustion of birth and death?

It is the consciousness of the eightfold path; seeing the truths and attaining the concentration on the truths constitutes these eight. Thus is the consciousness of practice for the cessation of the desire for birth and death.
What is the consciousness of the flavor of birth-and-death?
It is the arising of pleasure and joyful intent due to the causes and conditions of birth-and-death; such is the consciousness of the flavor of birth-and-death.
What is the consciousness of the affliction of birth-and-death?
All that is subject to birth and death, impermanent, ending in suffering, and subject to change—this is the consciousness of the affliction of birth and death.
What is the essential consciousness of birth and death?

That which, regarding birth and death, through desire and craving, by means of desire and craving, is able to sever desire and is able to cross over—it is this that is the essential consciousness of birth and death.
“What is the aggregate of consciousness?
It is the consciousness of the six sense-bases: the consciousness of the eye-base, and the consciousness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases; such is the aggregate of consciousness.
What is the origination of consciousness?”
The conditioning of name-and-form is the conditioning of consciousness; thus, there is the conditioning of consciousness.
What is the exhaustion of consciousness through the exhaustion of formations?
The exhaustion of name-and-form is the exhaustion of consciousness; thus, there is the exhaustion of consciousness.
What is the practice for the exhaustion of consciousness?

There are eight modes of practice: right view up to right concentration as the eighth. Thus, this is the practice for the exhaustion of desire for consciousness, which is the consciousness that accords with reality.
What is the knowledge of the gratification (*āsvāda*) of consciousness regarding what is cognized?
It is the arising of pleasure and the arising of joy in the mind due to causes and conditions; such is the gratification, and it is known as the arising of gratification.
What is the knowledge of the affliction (*ādīnava*) of consciousness?
That which is cognized as exhaustion, as suffering, and as turning away—such is the cognition that troubles cognition.
What is essential cognition?
That which is cognized as the desire-and-lust for what is cognized, as the ability to overcome desire-and-lust, and as the ability to transcend it—such is essential cognition.
"In this way, bhikṣus,
there are seven points for awakening to. What are the seven?
Form has the seven matters of arising, cessation, the flavor of the path, suffering, and the essential. These five aggregates each possess these seven matters.
What are the three contemplations?

Consciousness also possesses these seven matters; by obtaining the five aggregates, one forms the six sense-bases (*āyatana*). Contemplating the body as the first form, contemplating the five aggregates as the second, and contemplating the six sense-bases as the third—therefore, they are called the three contemplations.

"Monks! One who can comprehend the seven bases and also practice the three contemplations will, before long, cultivate the path and sever the fetters. Being free from the intention of fettering, liberated and wise, seeing the path and seeing the essential, they realize the single cessation; having severed the mental formations of birth and death, their task is finished, and they shall no longer return to the cycle of birth and death, having attained the Way."
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four attachments. What are the four?
First is attachment to desire, second is attachment to the world, third is attachment to views, and fourth is attachment to delusion.

There are also four ways of being free from such attachment: freedom from attachment to desire, freedom from attachment to the world, freedom from attachment to views, and freedom from attachment to delusion.
He spoke further, saying: "One who desires to see is bound by delusion;

for this reason, one remains in the world and through this receives a body. If one can abandon desire, one may also leave the world; seeing will be severed, and delusion will be extinguished. Thus one attains the bliss of vision while remaining in the world, being unconditioned and free from all attachments; no longer attached, one no longer follows the cycle of birth and death."
Thus spoke the Buddha. (5) It was heard thus:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four inversions of thought, and the same applies to views.

From these inversions, people become deluded, entangled, and mentally fabricated; they perceive non-going as going. Thus they afflict themselves in this life and the next, dwelling in the world within birth and death, unable to escape."
What are the four? First, to regard the impermanent as permanent; this constitutes a perversion of thought, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view.
Second, to regard suffering as pleasure.
"Third, taking what is not the body to be the body;
fourth, taking what is impure to be pure—these constitute the inversions of thought, intention, and view.
The subsequent teaching concludes:

"To regard what is impermanent as permanent, to contemplate suffering as pleasure, to take what is not the self as the self, and to see the impure as pure—such are the inversions. When mental karma is thus perverted, one abandons what is beneficial and pursues what is harmful; this leads now to old age and death."

It is like a mother cow with her calf. Since there is already a Buddha in the world, he reflects upon the heavens above and the earth below, having attained the eye of the Way to cross over the world. He then perceives this Dharma which eliminates all suffering; he also explains that suffering arises from birth and teaches how to transcend suffering. He further perceives the eightfold noble path leading to the Deathless (*amṛta*). Having heard this Dharma, one then perceives impermanence, suffering, and non-self; seeing that the body is impure, one becomes free from fear. One attains the vision of bliss in the world, realizes the Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and crosses over the world from all afflictions without attachment.
Thus spoke the Buddha. (6) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four kinds of giving that cause people to become like-minded. What are these four?
First is giving; second is mutual affection; third is benefit; and fourth is sharing in benefits.
Regarding the first, what is explained as giving?
There is no supreme giving that exceeds the Dharma.

The second is loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which does not exceed its proper measure; hearing the sutras also opens the mind. The third is beneficial action (*hita*), which does not exceed its proper measure:

it causes those who lack faith to have faith; it teaches others to ascend [to higher states]; it causes those who do not observe the precepts to observe them; it causes those who do not study to study; it causes the stingy to practice giving; it causes the foolish to become wise; and it leads others into the right path.

The fourth is sharing in benefits; there is no one who shares in benefits more perfectly than an Arhat, and it is likewise for an Anāgāmin, a Sakṛdāgāmin, and a Srotāpanna; those who uphold the precepts share in these benefits.
The subsequent discourse was thus concluded. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"There are four wheels of the Dharma that cause both devas and humans to practice according to them. If one falls among humans or devas, by practicing these wheels of the Dharma, one shall become honored and preeminent, following the practice of wholesome dharmas."
What are the four? First, associating with virtuous people;
second, relying on the wise.
"Third is the knowledge of the truths and vows;
fourth is having performed meritorious deeds in past lives.
Thus it concludes from the latter [section]:
"Those who dwell well among the virtuous, who know the truths and aspire to their past lives, shall find joy and be free from sorrow, attaining mastery over the wholesome.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
(8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four classes of people.

There are those who protect themselves but do not protect others; there are those who protect others but do not protect themselves; there are those who neither protect themselves nor protect others; and there are those who both protect themselves and protect others.”
Thus spoke the Buddha. (9) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are four classes of persons.

There is the person who protects their own body but does not protect the bodies of others; there is the person who protects the bodies of others but does not protect their own body; there is the person who neither protects themselves nor protects others; and there is the person who both protects themselves and protects others."
One who protects neither themselves nor others is the most base of persons;
one who protects others but not themselves is superior;
and one who protects themselves but not others is also superior.
"To protect oneself and also to protect others is supreme;
such a person is the most foremost.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
10 (Ten). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four kinds of clouds: the first has only thunder but no rain;
the second has only rain but no thunder;
the third has neither rain nor thunder.”
The fourth type of cloud has both rain and thunder.
To use a metaphor of clouds, there are likewise four classes of people: the first class of people has only thunder but no rain.
Second, there is only rain without thunder;
third, there is neither thunder nor rain;
fourth, there is both thunder and rain.
What kind of person is like one who has thunder but no rain? Here, a certain bhikṣu merely recites the sūtras;

he speaks well at the beginning, speaks well in the middle, and speaks well at the conclusion. His discourse is analytical and emphasizes the essential practice and the essential vision; yet he himself does not know the Dharma, nor does he know the Dharma as it accords with its practice. Such a person is said to have only thunder but no rain.

What is meant by "there being only rain and no thunder"? It refers to those people in this world who do not preach the Dharma-sūtras; they do not speak of what is good at the beginning, nor in the middle, nor at the conclusion. They lack the discernment of practice, nor do they fulfill the requirements of practice or perceive its essential goal. Rather, their intention lies solely in practicing within the Dharma—practicing with harmony and benefit, acting in accordance with the Dharma, receiving the Dharma and practicing according to it, and following the Dharma in their conduct. Such a person is one for whom there is only rain and no thunder.
What is meant by "there being neither rain nor thunder"? It refers to one who does not preach the sūtras;

who does not speak of what is good at the beginning, does not speak of what is good in the middle, and does not speak of what is good at the conclusion; who does not provide detailed analysis, nor speak of the complete practice of the essentials of goodness; who does not personally understand the wholesome dharmas, nor personally practice the realization of the Dharma. Such a person is said to have neither rain nor thunder.
What is meant by "there is both rain and thunder"? It refers to a person here who preaches the Dharma of the sutras;

they preach what is good at the beginning, what is good in the middle, and what is good at the end; they preach what is good in their analysis and what is good in their essential practice. They understand the Dharma through the Dharma as it arrives, they speak of conduct, and they attain mastery in the understanding of the Dharma. Having reached the Dharma, they also personally understand and comprehend its practice. Such a person is one for whom there is both rain and thunder.
Thus spoke the Buddha. (11) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four abodes. What are the four?"
First is the relinquishing of the dwelling, second is guarding the dwelling, third is protecting the dwelling, and fourth is practicing the relinquishment of the dwelling.
What is meant by the relinquishing of the dwelling?

It is to mindfully not accept what comes, and through non-clinging, to clearly understand and remain far removed from it; likewise, even if one is met with anger or deception, through non-clinging, one clearly understands and remains far removed from it. This is called the relinquishing of the dwelling.
What is meant by "guarding the dwelling"?
When the eye has already seen a form, one does not grasp its signs nor contemplate its signs; yet, if from causes and conditions there arises what is unwholesome, one guards against it.
If one perceives delusion through causes and conditions, or perceives what is disagreeable through causes and conditions, or perceives the arising of malicious intent through causes and conditions,
one should then personally maintain and practice merit, guarding the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
To not grasp at signs in accordance with the Dharma, as explained above, is called "guarding the dwelling" (*śālā-rakṣā*).
What is "protecting the dwelling"?

Here, a bhikṣu has already produced various wholesome signs regarding the body: such as the lividness and swelling of a corpse, or being half-eaten by foxes or dogs, or bleeding red, or turning blue-black and putrid, or the whiteness of bones, or the skull; he gazes upon these with mature discernment, skillfully protecting them so that his mind does not lose these wholesome signs—this is called "protecting the dwelling."
What is the cultivation of equanimity (*upekṣā*)?

Here, a bhikṣu, because he has become detached from the mental applications of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), because he has distinguished them, and because he has analyzed and distanced himself from them, thus arrives at the contemplation of the mental applications of awakening; this is called the cultivation of equanimity.
He concluded his teaching from the end:

"To dwell, to guard, to protect, and to practice—these are called the four abodes. It is thus that the Noble One speaks; practicing these without ceasing, one brings an end to suffering and attains the Way."
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the disciples rose, paid homage to the Buddha, and received his teaching for practice. (12) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu possesses four practices, he will not harm himself and will surely draw near to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
What are these four?..."

In this regard, a bhikṣu maintains the precepts and practices within the discipline; he guards the sense-faculties up to the guarding of the mind; he observes moderation in eating, neither eating excessively nor delighting in excessive eating; and throughout the first and last watches of the night, he constantly maintains his practice—these are the four practices.
"A bhikṣu does not harm himself and draws near to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Following this, he spoke further:

"If a bhikṣu establishes the roots of virtue (*śīla-mūla*), practices moderation in eating, maintains mindfulness (*saṃprajanya*), and does not abandon vigilance, practicing diligence in this way, he shall not cease his efforts during the first or last watch of the night."
"One must not diminish oneself; one must draw near to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Thus spoke the Buddha. 13 (13) It was heard thus:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
“If a worthy person dwells at home practicing the Dharma, they will bring joy to four families.”

What are the four? First, parents, wives, and children; second, sons, guests, servants, and slaves; third, acquaintances, relatives, and friends; fourth, kings, celestial kings, spirits, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas.
He continued from there, saying:

"Parents, as well as śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and likewise the deities of the shrines—those who believe in these shrines at home, for the sake of such people, are able to serve their precept-observing relatives; furthermore, those people who are currently living do not offend the relatives of the Heavenly King, and all people themselves also receive his grace."

Thus it is for one who dwells with wisdom; by hearing of and practicing wholesome deeds, they attain greatness. This is also called "renown in the present life," which can never be fully described, and leads to rebirth in the heavens in a future life.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
14 (Fourteen). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, another brāhmaṇa approached the Buddha; having approached him, he inquired after the Buddha’s well-being, and having inquired after his well-being, he then asked the Buddha:
"For what cause and condition, worthy one,
do people in the world today have little beauty, lack strength, suffer much from illness, have short lifespans,
and are not very powerful? The Buddha replied to the brahmin:

"In this present age, the Brahmins are unrighteous and covetous for worldly things; they perversely act upon their intentions and fall into unrighteousness. Because these people defile themselves with such thoughts and fall into unrighteousness, and because they perversely fall into greed rather than practicing what is right, by reason of these causes and conditions, the sun and moon do not move in their proper courses.
Once they do not move in their proper courses, the constellations likewise do not move in their proper courses.
Once the constellations do not move in their proper courses, the sun and moon become irregular, and the seasons and years likewise become irregular."
When the seasons have become irregular, the divisions of time by water-clock measures become incorrect;
when the divisions of time by water-clock measures are incorrect, violent winds arise;
when violent winds arise, the heavens do not send down rain at the proper times.
Furthermore, O Brahmin, when the rains do not fall at the proper time, it is as if a person sows seeds in the ground at the wrong time;

they will ripen and mature unseasonably and fail to meet expectations. When crops ripen unseasonably, whether humans, livestock, or birds consume them, they will have little physical luster, little strength, much illness, short lifespans, and little vitality. This, O Brahmin, is the consequence.
"This was originally due to causes and conditions; nowadays, people of this world have little beauty, little strength, much illness, short lifespans, and little nobility.
Then the brahmin bowed his head in prostration before the Buddha and said:
"I have now awakened to this knowledge. From this day forward, I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, and I take refuge in the Saṅgha of bhikṣus."
Thus the Buddha taught. (15) It was heard thus:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are five auspicious occasions for giving.
What are these five auspicious occasions?

First is giving to those who have come from afar; second is giving with the desire to depart; third is giving when one is ill or emaciated; fourth is giving during times of famine; fifth is giving upon tasting something new—before eating it oneself, one should first give it to those who uphold the precepts and practice the path, and only afterwards eat it oneself for the sake of merit.
The discourse concludes:

"The wise person gives at the proper time with faith; in their practice, they harbor no stinginess. Giving at the proper time to a worthy person with a pure mind and free from doubt, their merit is immeasurable."
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus received and practiced his teaching with joy. 16 (16) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"Worthy ones, there are five kinds of giving. What are the five?
First, giving with faith as a virtuous person; second, giving in abundance; third, giving with one's own hands; fourth, giving at the proper time; and fifth, giving without encroaching upon others.
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus:
"What kind of merit is obtained from giving with faith?

One who gives with faith will obtain great wealth; they will possess abundant property, many precious jewels, many desirable things, and many fine articles. Furthermore, people of the world will place their trust in such a person. This, bhikṣus, is the merit of giving with faith."
What is meant by "giving much"?

As explained above, one receives love, respect, and veneration from one's parents; likewise, one receives respect and veneration from one's brothers, from one's wife and children, from one's servants and slaves, and from one's friends and neighbors. Thus, all five types of relatives show respect and veneration; this is how a bhikṣu gives much merit.
By giving with one's own hand, what kind of wealth does one obtain through such giving?

As explained above, one obtains whatever one desires within the household; one obtains the finest garments, the finest bedding and seating, and finds pleasure according to one's own will. One finds pleasure according to one's own will regarding forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures. This bhikṣu obtains merit from giving with his own hand.
What is giving at the proper time and giving merit?

Giving at the proper time and giving merit means that, as previously described regarding wealth, when one’s life is about to end and one’s property, treasures, and possessions are present before one, they remain as desired without scattering in all directions; this is a bhikṣu’s giving at the proper time and giving of merit.
What is the merit of a bhikṣu practicing generosity without encroaching upon others?

Regarding the practice of generosity without encroaching upon others through the observance of precepts: it results in wealth as described above. Furthermore, if one engages in productive labor with diligence, exerting effort from one's own arms and enduring the hardships of cold to achieve success, then no one can forcibly seize that merit. Neither government officials, thieves, water, nor fire can cause harm to it, nor is there any expenditure that is undesirable; this is the merit of a bhikṣu practicing generosity without encroaching upon others.

He spoke further: "Faithful one, when giving with one's own hands at the proper time, not encroaching upon others, the wise person practices such generosity. From such giving, one obtains boundless happiness; likewise, the performance of merit is also distinguished."
Thus spoke the Buddha. (17) It was heard thus:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a person’s mind remains within five dharmas, even if they hear the teachings of the Buddha-dharma, they shall not remove the dust and defilements, nor shall they attain the eye of the Path."

What are these five? First, to disturb one who preaches the sūtra; second, to seek out their vulnerabilities; third, to seek to exhaust them with questions; fourth, upon hearing [the teaching], to harbor wrong thoughts and fixate on external causes and conditions; and fifth, to lack the humility that prevents one from discriminating between the superior and the inferior based on what has been heard.

"If a person's mind follows these five dharmas, even if they hear the Buddha preach the Dharma, they will not be able to personally cleanse their defilements, nor will they be able to give rise to the Dharma-eye.
The Buddha further addressed the bhikṣus:

"There are five other dharmas; if a person's mind dwells in these five dharmas, then upon hearing the Buddha teach the practice of the Dharma, they will be able to personally cleanse their defilements and shall also attain the Path-eye."
What are these five?
First, one harbors no ill will toward the one who expounds the sutra;
second, one seeks neither the faults nor the merits within the sutra, but ceases inquiry once a doubt has been resolved.
Third, the mind does not dwell on form, nor does the mind dwell on other causes and conditions;
fourth, one possesses an inherently discerning mind capable of understanding good and evil;
fifth, one distinguishes and knows for oneself.
These are the five dharmas.

If a person’s mind conforms to these five dharmas, they will be able to liberate themselves from defilements: first, not troubling the one who preaches the sūtra; second, not seeking out the faults or merits within the sūtra; third, not seeking to exhaust [the teaching]; fourth, not harboring wrong thoughts; and fifth, possessing a wise mind oneself that can distinguish between the white and the black.
Thus spoke the Buddha. (18) It was heard thus:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
“One sees the one through five practices. What are these five?”

If a practitioner is one who practices, they should contemplate this body from head to hand and foot—from the hair on top of the head, the skull, and the skin—as being filled with various kinds of impure characteristics. They observe that this body contains hair, body hair, nails, teeth, blood vessels, muscle, tendons, bones, the spleen, kidneys, large intestine, small intestine, stomach, rectum, feces, urine, tears, sweat, nasal mucus, saliva, liver, lungs, heart, gallbladder, blood, fat, marrow, wind, heat, and the crown of the head. To maintain such a reckoning is called the first stage of mindfulness, the arrival at seeing the one.
If a practitioner further calculates as described above, with the mind unmoving in the mental attention as described above, this is the second practice of seeing of the worthy one.
If a practitioner further contemplates this, as described above regarding feeling, consciousness, and formations, and calculates whether this consciousness belongs to the present life?
Or for future lives? If a practitioner holds such a thought, this constitutes the first view of the third practice.

If a practitioner reflects and calculates as described above—that they calculate and contemplate that consciousness has no place of rest in either this life or future lives—and if the practitioner awakens to this calculation, this constitutes the first view of the fourth practice.

If a practitioner calculates as described above—that there is a person who possesses consciousness and conceives of this matter—then that person has no place of rest in either the present life or future lives, and thus fails to attain even a single pure contemplation. If a practitioner holds such a conceptual understanding and makes this calculation, it constitutes the fifth view regarding the purity of practice and the perception of unity.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
(19) It was heard thus: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
“Bhikṣus, there are five causes and conditions that cause the eye of a person not to rest,
giving rise to delusion, destroying wisdom, and causing affliction for people, so that they cannot attain the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).”
What are the five? First, sensual desire; second, ill will; third, sloth and torpor; fourth, restlessness and remorse; and fifth, doubt and lack of faith.
Thus spoke the Buddha. (20) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are five virtues in walking on foot. What are these five?

First, one is able to run; second, one possesses strength; third, it dispels drowsiness; fourth, food is easily digested and does not cause illness; fifth, it is easy for the practitioner to attain concentration of mind, and once concentration is attained, it endures for a long time.
Thus spoke the Buddha. (21) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu practices five dharmas, he can dwell on mountains or in marshes, and can lie down upon a bed of grass."
What are the five?
First, being able to uphold the precepts without transgression, gathering and guarding the training rules;
second, being likewise able to gather the sense-doors and maintain their conduct.

Third, one is also able to practice diligence and possesses the power of diligence; remaining close to the essential without departing from it, one does not abandon diligence until the attainment of the Way.
Fourth, having received the Buddha’s discipline, one understands it for oneself.
Fifth, upon hearing the sutras, one easily understands their true meaning.
"If a practitioner accepts these five dharmas as explained above, he will be able to dwell upon a mountain or in a marsh.
Thus spoke the Buddha. (22) It was heard thus:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda: "All things, Ānanda!"
"I say that one must not commit evil with the body; the same applies to speech and mind.
Ānanda then addressed the Buddha:
"If one commits no evil with body, speech, or mind, and a person refrains from performing such acts, how much evil does one avoid by virtue of this?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"It is due to the five evils. What are these five?"

First, one deceives oneself; second, one also deceives others; third, when speaking, one's words do not accord with the intentions of the noble ones above or below; fourth, one’s reputation is not heard throughout the ten directions; and fifth, after death, one falls into hell.
The Buddha again addressed Ānanda:
"Ānanda, all wholesome actions of body—I teach that these should be performed; the same applies to speech and mind."
Ānanda spoke again:
"The Buddha has taught that one should practice all wholesome deeds of body as I instruct, and likewise for speech and mind.
If a person practices these deeds, how much merit might they expect to obtain?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"It brings five blessings.
What are the five? "

First, not to deceive oneself; second, likewise not to deceive others; third, for one's speech to be worthy of the approval of the noble; fourth, for one's fame to spread throughout the ten directions; fifth, for one to ascend to the heavens after death.
Thus spoke the Buddha. 23 (23) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are five afflictions that people can tolerate when they depend upon one another. What are these five?
If monks rely on one another, they may at times rely on what is faulty, and thus the Saṃgha of monks does not wish to see them;
yet when they go out and rely on others, those they relied upon think, "Those whom we relied upon have now gone out and do not wish to see us."
Becoming attached in mind, he did not wish to go to the assembly of monks, thinking, "Why should I ever go to the assembly of monks again?
Thus, he no longer went; having ceased going, he no longer saw the assembly of monks;
having ceased seeing the assembly of monks, he no longer heard the Dharma.
Having not heard the Dharma, one does not fall into the Dharma, departs from the Dharma, and does not abide in the Dharma;

this is the first way a bhikṣu causes distress to people, who depend upon one another. Second, there is also the case where a person is beloved by a bhikṣu, yet that beloved person commits a transgression. When the bhikṣus assemble, the one with the transgression is seated at the very bottom of the assembly. Then the beloved one thinks to himself: "Because my beloved has been seated at the very bottom of the bhikṣu assembly, I shall no longer go to the bhikṣu assembly. [The thought] that because he is seated at the very bottom of the bhikṣu assembly, he will no longer go to the bhikṣu assembly, is as explained above. The middle case is also as stated above.
Third, carrying one's alms bowl and kashaya robe to another country;
fourth, abandoning the precepts to become a layperson;
fifth, sitting in self-reproach over the loss of reputation, as described above.
Thus spoke the Buddha. (24) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are five evils for one who does not endure with patience. What are these five?

First, having many enemies; second, being subject to much slander; third, having much that is disagreeable; fourth, having one's evil conduct ill-reputed throughout the ten directions; and fifth, at the end of life, falling into the miserable hells—these are the five evils for those who do not practice patience.
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus:

"There are five benefits for one who possesses wholesome patience: they will have no enmity; they will have no slander; they will have nothing disagreeable; they will have a reputation throughout the ten directions; and when their life ends, they will be reborn in the heavens."
Thus spoke the Buddha. (25) It was heard thus:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are five evils, O bhikṣus! A person who cannot endure practice; a person who cannot endure practice."

What are the five? First, being coarse due to intolerance; second, having a quick temper; third, harboring resentment thereafter; fourth, lacking loving-kindness and abounding in hatred; fifth, falling into hell at the end of one's life and body.
The opposite of these constitutes purity.
Thus spoke the Buddha. (26) It was heard thus:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"An elephant possesses five characteristics that make it worthy of office, fit for the King's use, pleasing to the King's mind, and capable of leading the King according to the Dharma."
What are the five?
First, being able to hear and receive; second, being able to abide; third, being able to contend; fourth, being able to run;
fifth, being able to guard oneself. What are these, bhikṣus?
How does the palace elephant guard itself?

If the elephant enters the midst of an army, its forefeet can fight while its hind feet, haunches, back, belly, shoulders, neck, and trunk can protect themselves; this is what is called guarding oneself.
If a bhikṣu possesses five conditions, he should pay homage to those of renown, he should receive the añjali-greeting from others, and his merit-ground will be inexhaustible.
What are these five?

Hearing and receiving constitute the first; the capacity [to receive] constitutes the second; the act of receiving constitutes the third; volitional formation constitutes the fourth; and guarding constitutes the fifth.
What are the flavors in the mouth, the subtle touches on the body, and the thoughts in the mind—how can one exercise restraint so as not to grasp at their characteristics?
Thus it is, bhikṣu!
A bhikṣu who is able to guard himself guards against the six decays (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

The second is dhyāna; the third, receiving [the teachings], is patience (*kṣānti*); the fourth is being able to uphold the precepts (*śīla*); and the fifth, receiving through hearing, is diligence (*vīrya*).

When a practitioner possesses these five qualities, they shall attain renown; they shall receive the salutation of joined palms from others; their merit and ground shall be inexhaustible; and disciples shall hear them and receive their teachings with satisfaction.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are five ways in which evil does not rely upon others. What are these five?

First, the mind of one who does not rely [on others] is not resolved; second, the mind of one who relies [on others] is crooked and estranged; third, one’s own mind is not resolved; fourth, one violates the practice of the Path; and fifth, one does not accept the Buddha’s solemn teaching.”

The five bases of goodness: relying on others, not being envious of them, understanding their intentions with a benevolent mind, understanding their minds without falling into confusion regarding one’s own mind, and practicing equanimity toward all people in the world while providing insight to those who come after.
Thus spoke the Buddha. (28) It was heard thus:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"All fears are what is called desire. Bhikṣus!"
That is to say, monks, all sufferings are called desire;
all diseases, monks, are called desire.
"Monks! These various fetters are what is called desire. Monks!"
“Monks, all sores are called desire; all mud is called desire.”
"Monks! All attachments are called desire. Monks!"
"All those who fall into a mother’s womb—this is called desire.
Bhikṣus! For what reason are all fears considered desire?"
Because worldly fools are overwhelmed by craving and bound by craving, they cannot escape various fears in the present life, nor can they escape them in future lives.
"Monks! For this reason, all fears are due to desire. Monks!"
Why is this? All sufferings are caused by desire.
Because foolish people of the world are led astray by craving and bound by craving, they cannot escape various fears in the present life, nor can they escape them in future lives.
"Monks! For this reason, all suffering is caused by desire. Monks!"
Why is this? All illnesses arise from desire.
Because worldly fools are overwhelmed and bound by craving, they fail to escape the various fears of the present life, nor can they escape them in future lives.
"Monks! For this reason, all illnesses are due to desire. Monks!"
Why is this? Because the various fetters constitute desire;
due to worldly deluded persons being led astray by craving and bound by craving, they fail to escape from all fears in the present life, nor can they escape them in future lives.
For this reason, the various fetters are called desire. "Monks!
For what reason are the various sores called desire?"
Because worldly fools are overwhelmed by greed and bound by greed, they fail to escape from all fears in the present life, nor shall they escape them in future lives.
"Monks! For this reason, all sores are caused by desire. Monks!"
Why is this? All defilements constitute desire.
Because foolish people of the world are led astray by greed and bound by greed, they cannot escape various fears in the present life, nor can they escape them in future lives.
"Monks! For this reason, all defilements are called desire. Monks!"
Why is this? All attachments constitute desire.
Because foolish people of the world are dissipated by craving and bound by craving, they cannot escape various fears in the present life, nor can they escape them in future lives.
"Monks! For this reason, all attachments are desire. Monks!"
Why is this? Those who enter a mother’s womb do so out of desire.
Because worldly fools are overwhelmed by greed and bound by greed, they cannot escape various fears in the present life, nor can they escape them in future lives.
"Monks! Therefore, all those who fall into a mother’s womb do so because of desire.
Having spoken thus, the Buddha then uttered this verse:

"Fearing suffering, illness, fetters, and sores—this is called desire. When a deluded person is bound by these, they enter the mother’s womb due to their attachment to form. As stated above, a bhikṣu who has understood with right mindfulness should not abandon the overcoming of all fears; as one of profound wisdom, he should cross over them and contemplate the successive cycles of birth, aging, and conditioned activity in the world."
At that time, the Buddha spoke thus: "There are eight kinds of sores:

first, the sore of doubt; second, the sore of craving; third, the sore of greed; fourth, the sore of hatred; fifth, the sore of delusion; sixth, the sore of pride; seventh, the sore of wrong views; eighth, the sore of birth and death."
29 (Twenty-nine). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then invited the bhikṣus, and when they had arrived, the Buddha spoke this parable:

“Monks, for a person there is the year of swelling; whatever years have accumulated, they constitute that which is swollen. There are nine orifices, nine pains, and nine leakages. From these orifices, from which they leak, drip, and flow out, there issues only impurity, there flows out only impurity. Truly it is evil, difficult, and loathsome that this swelling issues forth and flows away.”

Monks, regarding this body as having four causal conditions—this body which is called "the body of four causal conditions"—it consists of nine apertures and nine pains; it is characterized by nine leakages that flow out, drip down, and run away, resulting only in the emission of impurity, only in the streaming of impurity, and only in the flowing and running forth of foul stench.
"Thus it is, bhikṣus!
This tumor of causes and conditions is something to be ashamed of, something to be feared, something to be dreaded, and something to be studied. Thus it is, bhikṣus!
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus received his teaching with joy and put it into practice.
30. The Sūtra on the Accumulation of Bones Spoken by the Buddha (30). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the kingdom of Rājagṛha. He then addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a person dwelling in this world were to collect the bones from their births and deaths throughout a single kalpa—preserving them so that they do not rot, decay, or perish—and were to pile them up until they were equal in height to Mount Sumeru; [this would be the measure of their suffering]."

"Among humans, there are those who undergo birth and death for a hundred kalpas, and there are those who undergo birth and death for a thousand kalpas, yet they are still unable to attain the Arhat path and Nirvana.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The bones of a person accumulated over the course of one kalpa would equal Mount Sumeru; it is for this reason that I manifest their original causes and conditions."

"Monks! You all must uproot their very foundations and depart from fundamental evil. For this reason, you shall no longer undergo birth and death; by no longer undergoing birth and death, you will attain the path of *nirvāṇa* that transcends the world."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
This is the *Sūtra on the Seven Bases and Three Contemplations* as spoken by the Buddha. (31) Regarding the Nine Untimely Deaths, it was heard thus:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are nine kinds of causes and conditions by which a person's life may end prematurely before its natural span is exhausted.
What are these nine?..."

First, eating at improper times; second, not measuring one's food; third, eating without practicing moderation in eating; fourth, failing to produce [wholesome roots]; fifth, stopping while the food is still being cooked; sixth, not maintaining the precepts; seventh, associating with evil friends; eighth, entering villages at improper times and acting contrary to the Dharma; ninth, failing to avoid what ought to be avoided.
"These are the nine causes and conditions by which a person's life is cut short prematurely.
When the bhikṣus heard the Buddha’s words, they rejoiced and paid homage.
"Who are those who should not be fed? [the bhikṣus asked].
That which is called "unpleasant food" refers to food that remains in the stomach without being digested; this is called "inappropriate food.
What is meant by "immoderate food"? It refers to not knowing moderation, eating more than is sufficient; this is called "immoderate food."
"What is meant by 'eating food that one has not practiced'?

It refers to not knowing the proper time; traveling to other regions during winter or summer, being ignorant of local customs, being unable to digest food and drink, and—because of this lack of practice—it is called eating food that one has not practiced."
"What is meant by 'not being expelled'?

It refers to when food has not yet been digested, yet more food is consumed on top of it; and because one does not take medicine to induce vomiting or purgation, it is not digested at the proper time—this is called 'not being expelled'."
"What is meant by 'maturing through restraint'?

It refers to not immediately going out when the urge for feces or urine arises; and restraining oneself when belching, vomiting, sneezing, or passing wind occurs—this is called maturing through restraint."
"What is meant by 'not upholding the precepts'? It refers to violating the five precepts:

killing, stealing, sexual misconduct with another's wife, double-tongued speech, and drinking intoxicants. Furthermore, there are other precepts; by violating them, one may enter the custody of the authorities, or die by force, or die by flogging, or receive a brand and subsequently die of starvation.

Or, even after escaping externally, one may be killed by enemies' hands; or, overcome by terror and reflecting on one's transgressions, one dies of grief. This is what is meant by not upholding the precepts."
"What is meant by 'associating with evil friends'?
They are called evil friends because they involve others in their own evil deeds. Why is this so?"

Because one does not distance oneself from evil associates while sitting, one fails to discern good from evil; one does not reckon with the wicked nature of evil associates, nor does one reflect upon their evil conduct—this is called being close to evil associates.
"What is meant by entering a village at an improper time? It refers to walking about in the darkness;

or walking about when there is clamor and dispute in the village; or encountering local officials and magistrates going out on a pursuit, yet failing to avoid what should be avoided; or entering a village and intruding into the houses of others; seeing what should not be seen, hearing what should not be heard, committing what should not be committed, speaking what should not be spoken, worrying over what should not be worried, and seeking what should not be sought—this is called entering a village at an improper time and acting contrary to the Dharma."
What is meant by "not avoiding that which should be avoided"?

It refers to not avoiding wild elephants, wild horses, charging oxen, speeding chariots, snakes, vipers, pits, wells, water, fire, drawn swords, intoxicated persons, wicked people, and various other such things; this is called not avoiding that which should be avoided.
“Monks! Such is the causal condition by which these nine types of persons, though their lives have not yet ended, shall meet their end through this very cause.

A wise person should recognize this and avoid such causal conditions; by avoiding them, one obtains two blessings: first, long life; second, by means of that long life, one is able to hear the excellent words and sublime teachings of the Way, and is likewise able to practice the Way.”
When the Buddha had spoken thus, they all received it with joy. (32) Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Two kinds of persons are difficult to find in the world. Which two? [The one who knows how to teach the Dharma and the one who knows how to practice it according to the teaching]."
"First, those who give first; second, those who are reciprocal and do not forget kindness.
Thus spoke the Buddha. (33) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Two kinds of persons are difficult to find in the world.”
"Who are these two people?
First, one who performs acts of kindness toward those toward whom it ought not to be done; second, one who receives kindness and repays that kindness.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
(34) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Two kinds of people are rarely found in the world. Which two?
First, those who attain what has been attained; second, those who attain that which is not yet attained and do not let it remain."
Thus spoke the Buddha. (35) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Two types of persons in the world are easily satiated.
Which two? [The answer follows:]"
"First is the attainment of the attainment-aggregate through guarding; second is the attainment of the attainment-aggregate through relinquishing.
Thus spoke the Buddha. (36) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Two kinds of persons are difficult to find in the world."
"Who are these two persons?
The first is one who is satisfied himself; the second is one who can satisfy others.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
(37) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Two kinds of persons are difficult to find in the world. Which two?
First, one who practices generosity with a mind free from regret; second, a bhikṣu who has attained the unconditioned through the correct path."
Thus spoke the Buddha. (38) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Two kinds of persons are difficult to find in the world. Which two? [The person who knows when they have heard what has not been heard, and the person who practices according to the Dharma as it has been taught.]"

First, one is free from the stingy mind; when managing the household, one gives with one's own hands and always delights in accomplishing the distribution of gifts through equal sharing. Second, the bhikṣu attains the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) through correctness.
Thus spoke the Buddha. (39) Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are two people in the world who are difficult to sever and difficult to overcome. Who are these two?"

First, while dwelling within a household, one should provide clothing, food, bedding, and medicine for illness as required; second, if a bhikṣu has no faith in or attachment to the household, he should abandon all bodily concerns, relinquish craving, and turn away from receiving [sensual objects] toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), never departing from the unconditioned.
Thus spoke the Buddha. (40) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Two pure and white dharmas enable one to contemplate the world.
What are these two?
The first is shame (*hrī*), and the second is modesty (*apatrāpya*).

If these two qualities did not exist in the world, it would be impossible to distinguish between father and mother, elder brother and younger brother, son and daughter, disciple and teacher, sovereign and noble person.

Even if there were such worldly improprieties—as for example, oxen, horses, elephants, chickens, pigs, and dogs are also animals—yet because one observes these two pure dharmas, and because of shame and modesty, one becomes clearly distinguished as father or mother, elder brother or younger brother, son or daughter, student or teacher, ruler or great person.

Even if there were such things as the impurities of this world—for example, oxen, horses, elephants, chickens, pigs, and dogs, which are also animals—it is only by observing that these phenomena are pure and white that one can achieve discernment.
Thus spoke the Buddha. (41) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"Abandon unwholesome conduct of the body. Why? Because by being able to abandon it, one attains liberation."
If one were unable to abandon unwholesome conduct of the body, the Buddha would likewise be unable to teach the abandonment of unwholesome conduct of the body.

Because it is possible to abandon unwholesome conduct of the body, I therefore teach the abandonment of unwholesome conduct of the body. One who does not abandon unwholesome conduct of the body will utterly lack wealth and property, and will likewise fail to practice giving; thus they fall into a double deprivation. Their eyes remain, yet they see nothing; from this state they fall into hell, where no eyes reach that place. One who does not restrain themselves is called "one-eyed."

Through theft, wicked conduct, double-tongued speech, and lying; possessing only wealth and seeking only worldly self-indulgence; resorting to what is unrighteous and to flattery for the sake of the Dharma; and amassing great riches yet neither enjoying them oneself nor giving them away—one has already fallen into the one-eyed hell.
The two eyes are the foremost of dharmas.

They lead to the cultivation of livelihood; one should eat what one possesses and also practice giving. From such conduct, one attains mastery over merit. Just as one who is unwise eats for oneself and also gives, so too, when one attains rebirth in the heavens, one is never separated from the Dharma.

There is no eye, nor is there but one eye; one should simply keep far away and not draw near. A wise person should merely calculate that the two eyes are the foremost for both this world and the world beyond.
Thus spoke the Buddha. (42) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Buddha was, and having arrived, he paid homage to the Buddha and addressed him, asking:
"World-Honored One, what is meant by 'the world' (*loka*)?
What is it that is called 'the world'?"
“Ānanda, this world consists of three:
first, the world of desire; second, the world of form; and third, the world of formlessness.
Furthermore, it is called ‘the world’ because it is that which brings about the retribution for the transgressions committed by persons.”
If, Ānanda, one wishes to bring about non-existence, there is no such thing; if one wishes for the world, there is likewise no such thing. Ānanda!
"The repayment to the Buddha does not depart from this.
The Buddha then addressed Ānanda: "It is so, Ānanda!"

Karma is the ground; consciousness is the seed; desire is the moisture; and ignorance is the darkness. When a person who is deluded lacks the eye of wisdom, they engage in unwholesome conduct; because of their unwholesomeness, their consciousness dwells in evil, and they fall into the world of desire.
"If, Ānanda, a person who practices through form does not reach form, it would not exist in the world.
The Buddha spoke again to Ānanda:
“Is it not thus? Ānanda then addressed the Buddha, saying,
“It is not apart from this.”
The Buddha again addressed Ānanda:

"This consciousness that proceeds through the stages of existence takes desire as its seed, craving and ignorance as its darkness; with ignorance and darkness as the middle, consciousness proceeds and comes to rest therein. This constitutes the worldly existence of form."
"Ānanda! Because one practices merit that is formless, there exists a world that is formless; if there were no practice of the formless, there would also be no world that is formless.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"It is not apart from this.
"By practicing in accordance with this, Ānanda, it becomes a field of merit.

Once the seed of consciousness has been moistened by craving and the darkness of ignorance, when a person is deluded, they lack the eye; because they do not fully comprehend the eye, there is no form. Consequently, the higher consciousness is termed the 'world without form.'"
Thus spoke the Buddha. (43) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus replied,
“So be it. The Buddha then spoke:
“There are three practices for one who has faith, by which one may purify the faith resulting from those practices.
What are the three?

First, the desire to see the enlightened ones; second, the desire to hear the sūtras; third, being free from the stain of stinginess, so that when dwelling at home, one distributes wealth directly with one’s own hands, thereby perfecting the intention of giving and the like.”
The subsequent verse concludes:
"Those who wish to see the Light / Should delight in hearing the sutras / And likewise eliminate defilements and stinginess;
/ This is what is called faith."
Thus spoke the Buddha. (44) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus replied,
“So be it. The Buddha then spoke:
“There are three kinds of peace, goodness, and happiness; if a wise person desires these, they should protect the precepts.

First, desiring that fame and the Dharma follow one another, one should protect the precepts. Second, desiring wealth, pleasure, and agreeable gifts, those who wish to obtain them should protect the precepts. Third, regarding this present body and seeking to transcend this world for the sake of the heavenly realms and wisdom in future lives, those who wish to attain these should protect the precepts.”
The discourse concludes as follows:

"The wise person should guard the precepts; desiring to attain the three aspirations, renown, and benefit for future lives, and desiring the bliss of the heavens—this is the basis for such speech. If the wise can practice these matters as described above, they shall obtain worldly happiness and purity."
Thus spoke the Buddha. (45) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
“In the world there are three great diseases, each of which exists within the human body.
What are these three?”
The first is wind, the second is heat, and the third is cold; these are the three great diseases.
Monks, there are three great medicines for them. Regarding wind, monks:
For the great disease of wind, sesame oil is the great medicine, as are those things belonging to the category of sesame oil.
For the great disease of heat, curd and ghee are the great medicines, as are those things belonging to the category of curd and ghee.
For the great disease of cold, honey is the great medicine, as are those things belonging to the category of honey.
These bhikṣus have three great diseases and these are the three great medicines.
Likewise, for humans there are also three diseases that arise together and dwell together; they are taught through the Dharma of the Path and its realization. What are these three?
The first is desire, the second is hatred, and the third is delusion. For these three great diseases of a bhikṣu, there are three great medicines:

for the great disease of desire, the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is the great medicine; for the great disease of hatred, the practice of universal loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the great medicine; for the great disease of delusion, the contemplation of dependent origination from its primary causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is the great medicine. These are the three medicines for the three great diseases of a bhikṣu.
Thus spoke the Buddha. (46) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are three roots of evil:
greed is the first root of evil, hatred is the second root of evil, and delusion is the third root of evil."

Taking greed as the root of evil, stinginess is likewise the root of greed; because of stinginess, one cannot escape stinginess, and thus one commits evil through bodily action, evil through verbal action, and evil through mental action—this is also called evil.
Because of stinginess, one does not truly accept oneself; this is a mind that does not truly accept itself, and it is also the root of evil.

Because of stinginess, one clings to stinginess, thereby destroying oneself and also destroying what is excellent about oneself; to destroy both is also evil. Because of stinginess, one lacks knowledge: one does not know oneself, nor does one know what is excellent; to lack knowledge of both is also evil.

To be attached through stinginess and, out of a desire for something extraordinary, to give by means of killing, imprisonment, binding, destruction, or debate—this is also evil. To be attached through stinginess and, out of a desire for something extraordinary, to give suffering as a gift—whether by killing, imprisoning, binding, destroying, or debating—and to experience joy in one's heart and attain one's wish—this too is evil.

Such a person, O bhikṣu, is called one who speaks at an improper time; he is also called one who speaks contrary to the Dharma and not according to the Dharma; he is also called one whose speech does not cease evil. Why is this?

“Monks! Such a person speaks at an improper time; he is also called one who does not cease from evil speech. Furthermore, monks, he deceives himself and, being foolish, increases his own folly. If someone speaks what is truthful, he knows that the truth will not be accepted. If someone speaks what is untruthful, he speaks unpleasantly and pathetically, whether it be right or wrong, saying ‘I do not have this. For this reason, such a person is called wicked; he speaks untruthfully, speaks improperly and disagreeably, and does not cease from evil speech.”

Such a person, O bhikṣu, has many instances of stinginess arising from the causes and conditions of stinginess; coarse and evil qualities arise from this, and the same applies to the arising of hatred and delusion.

Such persons, from this point onward, will not remain for long; driven by greed, hatred, and delusion, they will be shrouded and overwhelmed by coarse, evil, and unrighteous conduct. Now that they have seen such teachings spoken to bring an end to suffering, they will further be beset by grief, affliction, and fear, their bodies ruined and their hopes dashed as they fall into evil states.

“Monks, it is as with a tree whose sprouts, roots, and shoots have been covered, concealed, filled, and sealed; so too, these various unwholesome states of greed, hatred, and delusion cover, conceal, fill, and seal themselves. Thus they constitute present suffering, and by ceasing in suffering, one brings grief and distress upon oneself and falls into evil states.”
“There are three roots of merit: first, the root of non-greed; second, the root of non-ill will; and third, the root of non-delusion. If one is not greedy, that is good;

if one is not stingy, and practices good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind, that too is good; if one truly accepts [the truth] with body, truly accepts it with speech, and truly accepts it with mind, that too is good.”
If one does not dwell on the offense against oneself, nor dwell on the offense against another, nor dwell on both offenses, this is also good.
If one is neither stingy nor associated with stinginess, whether through knowledge of oneself, knowledge of another, or knowledge of both, this is also good.

Whether one is not stingy, or whether one is connected or not, or whether one is extraordinary or not—if a person experiences suffering and grief, it would be better if they were made to exist [only] through being killed, or cut, or beaten, or slandered, or ruined, or through debate; even that would be preferable.

If one is not stingy, does not cling to stinginess, and does not cause wonder; if others are distressed, one does not cause them to suffer through killing, cutting, beating, slandering, causing loss, or contentious debate; if the mind does not accept such things, but remains joyful and causes wonder, so that others have their wishes fulfilled—this too is excellent.
Such a person is called one who speaks at the proper time, speaks truthfully, speaks with benefit, speaks according to the Dharma, and speaks for the restraint of evil;
this is also excellent.
Why is that? O Bhikṣus!

Such a person is called one who speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true, speaks according to the Dharma, and speaks to restrain evil; they know their own state of mind and the states of others, neither concealing nor hiding them.

If one knows oneself to be foolish, arrogant, or possessed of other such traits, and perceives that others are speaking of these, one should not conceal them; upon hearing their words, one should not say, "I do not know. Or, if someone engages in debate without sincerity, one should immediately clarify one's own mind and respond regarding the matter: "I have no lack of sincerity; there is nothing of mine, nor is there anything for the sake of 'me'. Therefore, when a person speaks at the proper time, speaks truthfully, speaks with merit, speaks according to the Dharma, and speaks to cease evil, they are not stingy, and the causes and conditions of such stinginess are likewise manifold.

Various wholesome dharmas lead from this state to the end of death without anger; likewise, they lead without delusion. Thus, there are many such bhikṣus who, having abandoned various forms of greed, anger, and delusion, as well as base and evil dharmas, do not give rise to them again. They dwell in peace within the Dharma, free from suffering, free from affliction, free from sorrow, and free from fever. Having destroyed the body, they look forward to a favorable rebirth.
By way of analogy, bhikṣus!
It is like a tree that has previously sprouted and grown; its shoots have spread out, covered it over, and closed it in completely.

Suppose a person comes and finds it impossible to remove the shoots, yet does not wish for them to remain, does not wish for them to be hidden, and does not wish for them to be pervasive; he would then dig up the roots and cut off the base.
Once the root is severed, the branches are severed;
once the branches are severed, they are shattered;
once they are shattered, they are split asunder.
Once split, it is quickly dried by the wind; once dried by the wind, it is burned by fire;
once burned by fire, it becomes ash;
once turned to ash, it is blown away by a great wind.
They are likewise cast into that river, becoming mere driftwood.

From this fundamental cause and condition, having already severed the root, they are no longer seen above or below; they will not arise again hereafter. In this way, O Bhikṣu, one reflects upon oneself through such analogies; those who practice the higher path are likewise not alone.

If greed, hatred, and delusion—those base and evil dharmas—have been abandoned and no longer arise, one dwells in peace seeing the Dharma; there is no suffering, no affliction, no sorrow, and no fever. Having destroyed the body, one then aspires for a superior rebirth.
Thus spoke the Buddha. (47) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
“These four practices are possessed by the wise and known by the noble ones; they are not known by the foolish, but are pleasing to those with discernment.”
What are the four? Monks,
giving is known by the wise, known by the noble, and approved by those possessed of discernment.
"O monks! Not to deceive is what all the world knows to be wise, as explained above;
and to serve one's parents with filial piety, O monks!"
That which is to be wisely known is as explained above;
being a śramaṇa, O bhikṣu!
that which is to be wisely known is as explained above.
"Monks, this practice of the Dharma is that which the wise know, which the noble ones know, and which fools do not know; it is for the wise to approve.
Thus it was said, concluding the discourse from behind.

"To know for oneself that one practices giving, is not deceitful, restrains the mind, maintains self-control, and is filial toward one's parents while upholding virtuous conduct—these matters are all the practice of the wise. When such things are seen to be accomplished, one attains pure aspirations in this world."
Thus spoke the Buddha. *The Scripture on the Seven Stations and Three Contemplations*, Fascicle One.
